# Introduction {#sec-introduction}

Every algorithm in the benchmark addresses the same task: given an instance of one of the problem families defined on the [Problem Definition](problem_definition.qmd) page, find a configuration of minimum energy. In frustrated systems the energy landscape contains many local minima separated by energy barriers, and low-lying minima may be far apart in configuration space. Algorithms therefore differ in how they balance two requirements: rapid descent toward low energies, and the ability to leave local minima that are not sufficiently deep.

Algorithms are contributed by **uploaders**. Each uploader has a folder `experiments/<uploader>/` in the [repository](https://github.com/ocadni/spin-glass-benchmarks/tree/main/experiments), which contains:

- the implementation of the algorithms;
- a `README.md` describing each algorithm: its **definition**, the **rationale** behind it, and the **configuration** of the reported runs;
- the results, which appear on the [Results](results.qmd) page under the same uploader name.

This page fixes the notation shared by all descriptions (@sec-notation) and lists every algorithm in the benchmark, with links to its description and implementation (@sec-list). The algorithms are grouped into **classes** according to their principle of operation. The benchmark currently includes two classes:

1.  **Zero-temperature descents**: Greedy, Reluctant, and Random descent, which only accept moves that lower the energy and terminate at a local minimum;
2.  **Annealing methods**: simulated annealing [@kirkpatrick1983sa], population annealing [@hukushima2003population; @machta2010population], and global annealing [@delbono2026; @delbono2025], which sample from a sequence of Boltzmann distributions at decreasing temperature.

The list of algorithms is not fixed. New algorithms are added either to an existing class or as a new class. See [Submit](submit.qmd) for how to contribute an algorithm and benchmark results.

# Notation and conventions {#sec-notation}

All algorithms in the benchmark operate on the pairwise Ising energy

$$
H(\mathbf{s})
= - \sum_{i<j} J_{ij} s_i s_j
  - \sum_{i} h_i s_i ,
\qquad s_i \in \{-1,+1\},
$$

with couplings and fields read from the instance files described in [File Format](file_format.qmd). For the SK model, the $1/\sqrt{N}$ normalization is included in the stored couplings. The **local field** acting on spin $i$ is

$$
h_i^{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbf{s}) = h_i + \sum_{j \neq i} J_{ij} s_j ,
$$

and the energy change produced by flipping spin $i$ alone is

$$
\Delta E_i(\mathbf{s}) = 2\, s_i\, h_i^{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbf{s}) .
$$

A spin with $\Delta E_i < 0$ is called **unsatisfied**: it is anti-aligned with its local field, and flipping it lowers the overall energy. A configuration with no unsatisfied spins is a **local minimum** with respect to single-spin flips. In frustrated systems the number of such minima grows exponentially with $N$, and typical local minima lie well above the ground state.

Algorithm descriptions use the following terms. A **sweep** consists of $N$ proposed single-spin updates, one per spin on average. Evaluating $\Delta E_i$ requires a sum over the neighbours of $i$, therefore a single sweep costs $O(N^2)$ operations on the complete SK graph and $O(N)$ on the EA3D lattice, where each spin has six neighbours. This difference should be kept in mind when comparing running times across families.
